title: Dalton Caldwell (YC): don't die, pivot toward what you know, avoid tarpit ideas
summary: Dalton Caldwell shares patterns from 1,000+ YC startups. Persistence beats cleverness, good pivots move closer to your expertise, tarpit ideas trap founders with false validation, and early founders should talk to customers in person instead of growth-hacking. He also covers why investors say no and the danger of over-delegating early.

principles.text: Keep going: nearly every big company had near-death moments where quitting looked rational.
principles.quote: there has to be this irrational you know intention to keep going even when the world tells you it's not working and you feel completely defeated and you likely have to go through this many times

principles.text: A good pivot moves closer to something you're an expert in and builds on what you learned from the prior idea.
principles.quote: usually a successful pivot gets warmer instead of Colder from what you're an expert at and somehow Builds on what you learned on the prior idea

principles.text: Pivot when you're out of growth ideas; stay the course while you still have many untried ones.
principles.quote: I would look at how many more ideas the founder has on how to make it grow like if it's not going well and you're out of ideas that is usually a good time to Pivot

principles.text: Tarpit ideas draw many founders with easy positive validation, so be wary of ideas everyone gravitates to.
principles.quote: part of being a true tarpit is that you can get good initial validation

principles.text: Talk to customers in person, spending 20-30% of your calendar on it, rather than hiding behind landing pages and ads.
principles.quote: look at your calendar and there should be you know 20 or 30% of your time that the calendar says something like customer meeting customer call

principles.text: Early-stage startups should skip growth hacking and analytics and get a first customer instead.
principles.quote: growth and growth hacking and doing all this analytics AB testing stuff um is a total waste of time for very early startups
